segments.text: Welcome to fascinating frontiers, episode 91, coming to you on June 4th, 2026.
Here's your space in science briefing. A meteorite from the Sahara holds the first
direct traces of a lost moon-size world that formed just after the solar system began.
The fragment contains isotopic signatures unlike any known asteroid or planet.
Researchers date its parent body to within a few million years of solar system formation.
The meteorite likely originated from a differentiated world roughly the size of the moon.
Its mineral structure points to early melting and core formation.
Laboratory measurements show the fragment once sat inside a moon-sized world
whose core and mantle separated before the object was destroyed.
Researchers are now comparing the sample against other primitive meteorites to map where this
lost world orbited. From ancient solar system relics, we turn to a telescope that will help us
understand the universe on its largest scales. The Nancy Gray's Roman space telescope will lift off
on August 30th aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. The observatory will serve a wide areas of the
sky to study dark energy, exoplanets, and infrared astrophysics. Engineers have completed final
instrument checks ahead of shipment to the launch site. A new blog will track mission milestones
and share images during commissioning. While Roman prepares to look outward, another long running
mission continues its close-up study of a neighboring planet. NASA leaders discussed recent operations
and science results from the Maven Orbiter during a public live stream. The mission has tracked atmospheric
loss at Mars for more than a decade. Data show how solar wind strips gases from the upper atmosphere
over time. The update covered instrument health after years in orbit. Future reports will detail
seasonal changes in the Martian exosphere. Mars' exploration on the surface is also sharpening its
aim at ancient water-rich terrain. New mapping shows clay layers at the Rosalind Franklin landing site
extend farther than earlier estimates. The deposits suggest a large body of water once covered
the region. Scientists believe these minerals could preserve organic molecules from ancient Mars.
The rover's drill will target these layers to search for chemical biosignatures. Orbital data from

distant galaxy cluster. The pair totals roughly 60 billion solar masses. The largest combined mass
reported. A 3,200 light-year-wide cavity surrounds the system, cleared by gravitational interactions.
The discovery came from deep imaging and dynamical modeling of the galaxy cluster.
The system offers a test bed for galaxy evolution models. While some objects are the biggest
ever seen, others are unexpectedly light and porous. Drop-tower tests at the University of
Duseberg-SN showed planetary simulant material expands under low gravity. The experiments simulated
conditions on small asteroids where self-gravity is weak. Results indicate surface material may be
less compacted than models assumed. If Earth's gravity were scaled down to that of a 10 kilometer
asteroid, a person could jump off the surface and never return. On such tiny worlds, the weak pull
allows loose grains to sit almost weightless, so even gentle vibrations or micrometri-right impacts
can make the top layer expand like foam. Experiments in a 100 meter drop-tower showed that the same
dry powder used to simulate asteroid dirt increased in volume by more than 30 percent once free-fall
removed its weight. That extra fluff changes how a spacecraft footpad sinks or how a drill bit
grips the surface. Yet no one has measured the exact porosity of the uppermost centimeters on
any visited asteroid. Leaving open the question of whether real surfaces are even lighter than the lab
results suggest. Closer to home, the evening sky offers a simple naked eye treat this week.
